title: South Asian kingdoms to 1000 CE
summary: Kingdoms of South Asia before 1000 CE: the Western Gangas of Karnataka, the Licchavis of Nepal, Zhangzhung in Western Tibet, the Hindu Shahis, the kingdoms of Sindh and Multan, the Vishnukundinas and Eastern Chalukyas of Andhra, the Kalachuris, the Chera Perumals, the dynasties of Odisha and Dakshina Kosala, the Later Guptas, the Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri and Porus.
dataNote: These are kingdoms that the base border data leaves out. Extents are approximate reconstructions from regional descriptions in the sources, trimmed to stay clear of the states the atlas already draws.

regions.name: Western Ganga kingdom (Gangavadi)
regions.capital: Kolar (Kuvalala), then Talakad (Talakadu) on the Kaveri from c. 390
regions.note: Gangavadi: the modern Mysore, Hassan, Mandya, Ramanagara, Chamarajanagar, Tumkur, Kolar and Bangalore districts (Wikipedia). Before c. 470 the kingdom held only the eastern districts round Kolar and Talakad; Sendraka (Chikkamagaluru, Belur), Punnata and the northern Kongu country were added by c. 470, and Kongu was held, contested with the Pandyas, into the 9th century. The Gangas were feudatories of the Badami Chalukyas (6th–8th c.) and, after a century of resistance, allies of the Rashtrakutas. After Takkolam (949) they were granted the Tungabhadra lands. Ended when the Cholas took Gangavadi c. 1000.
regions.dataNote: Before c. 470 only the eastern districts round Kolar and Talakad are drawn. The Gangas are drawn as their own kingdom throughout. The Tungabhadra lands granted after Takkolam (949) are not drawn. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

regions.name: Licchavi kingdom of Nepal
regions.note: The kingdom centred on the Kathmandu Valley; settlement reached east towards Banepa, west towards Tistung and north-west towards Gorkha. Dates c. 400–879; the dynasty was followed by the Thakuris. Tibet claimed overlordship in the mid-7th century.
regions.dataNote: Extent from Wikipedia: Licchavi (kingdom). The outer limits in the hills are a convention. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

regions.name: Zhangzhung
regions.capital: Khyunglung Ngulkhar ("Silver Palace of Garuda"), upper Sutlej valley south-west of Mount Kailash

rulers.name: Ligmikya (Lig-myi-rhya)
rulers.when: last king; killed in an ambush by Songtsen Gampo's men, c. 634–645

regions.note: Tibetan tradition makes Zhangzhung the whole of Western Tibet, Ladakh with Lahaul and Spiti, and Gilgit; Wikipedia (citing Stein) says how far it stretched is unknown. The start date (c. 500 BCE) rests on late Bon tradition and tentative Iron Age finds, not on contemporary records. The Tang Annals say Yangtong (Zhangzhung) submitted to Tibet in 634; Stein dates the conquest to 645.
regions.dataNote: Drawn here as Western Tibet (Ngari), Ladakh and Spiti only; Gilgit is left out. Where the Tibetan Empire is already drawn (from 623) this region gives way to it. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

regions.name: Hindu Shahi kingdom
regions.capital: Kabul, then Udabhanda (Hund) on the Indus

rulers.name: Bhimadeva
rulers.when: took Ghazni c. 963, end of reign c. 964

regions.note: Kabulistan, Gandhara and northern Punjab, between Kashmir to the east and the Samanids and Ghaznavids to the west. Kabul was lost to the Saffarids in 870 and regained c. 880–900. The Shahis lost the lands west of the Indus in 1001 and fell in 1026.
regions.dataNote: The region starts in 875 because the atlas's "Turk Shahis" realm, which Cliopatria labels Kabul Shahi, runs on to 874 and already stands for the Shahi kingdom in 822–874. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

rulers.name: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn Munabbih

rulers.name: Abu Lahab al-Munabbah ibn Asad al-Qurashi

regions.name: Rai kingdom of Sindh

rulers.name: Rai Sahiras II
rulers.when: killed fighting the Sasanian governor of Nimroz

regions.note: Known almost only from the 13th-century Chach Nama; no inscriptions survive and its reliability is debated (Wikipedia: Rai dynasty). Its realm was Sindh with the Multan district, its northern province, with claims towards Makran and Kashmir.

regions.name: Kingdom of Sindh (Chach dynasty)
regions.note: Chach, minister of the last Rai king, took the throne c. 632; his son Dahir was killed by the Umayyad army of Muhammad ibn al-Qasim in 712. The main source is again the Chach Nama.
regions.dataNote: Sindh and Multan are drawn; Makran is not. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

regions.name: Vishnukundina kingdom
regions.capital: Indrapalanagara (Nalgonda) according to some historians, then Denduluru near Eluru; also Amaravati
regions.note: Coastal Andhra between the Krishna and the Godavari, with Nalgonda and the Guntur country taken from the Ananda Gotrikas. Dated c. 420–624, ended by Pulakeshin II's conquest of Vengi.

regions.name: Eastern Chalukya kingdom of Vengi
regions.capital: Pishtapura (Pithapuram), then Vengi (Pedavegi near Eluru), later Rajamahendravaram
regions.note: Vengi, the delta country between the Krishna and the Godavari, with Pithapuram to the north-east. Began as the Badami Chalukya viceroyalty of 624 and became independent, probably after 642; Rashtrakuta armies overran it more than once in the 8th–9th centuries. Continued after 1000 under Chola protection.
regions.dataNote: Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.
